title: NumPy Binomial and Poisson Distributions
learningObjectives: Explain the concepts behind numpy binomial and poisson distributions.
Choose an appropriate NumPy random generator method and its parameters.
Use seeded generators for reproducible examples and tests.
Validate sample shape, range and data type.
Describe the assumptions and limitations of a finite random sample.

understand.concept: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability. The Poisson distribution models counts over a fixed interval when events occur at a constant average rate under its assumptions. NumPy Generator.binomial and Generator.poisson produce integer samples.
understand.whyItMatters: These distributions are useful for modeling repeated yes/no outcomes and event counts, while making their assumptions explicit.
understand.analogy: A random generator is like a repeatable deck-shuffling machine: a starting seed and the sequence of operations determine the generated sequence.
understand.summary: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability. explain.narrative: Run the examples and inspect the sample properties. A random sample is not a promise of exact theoretical frequencies; tests should focus on stable properties such as shape, valid range and reproducibility. examples.title: Draw binomial samples
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
x = rng.binomial(n=10, p=0.5, size=100)
print(x.shape, int(x.min()) >= 0, int(x.max()) <= 10)
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates draw binomial samples with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Count successes in one experiment
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
successes = rng.binomial(n=20, p=0.25)
print(0 <= successes <= 20)
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates count successes in one experiment with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Draw Poisson event counts
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
counts = rng.poisson(lam=4, size=200)
print(counts.shape, bool(np.all(counts >= 0)))
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates draw poisson event counts with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Use a different Poisson rate
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
counts = rng.poisson(lam=12, size=50)
print(counts.dtype.kind in 'iu', counts.size)
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates use a different poisson rate with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Check count-valued output
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
x = rng.binomial(5, 0.4, size=30)
y = rng.poisson(2.5, size=30)
print(bool(np.all(x == np.floor(x)) and np.all(y == np.floor(y))))
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates check count-valued output with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

questions.prompt: What does a seeded NumPy Generator provide?
questions.answer: A reproducible pseudo-random sequence when the generator and call sequence are the same.
options: A truly random sequence that can never repeat.
A reproducible pseudo-random sequence when the generator and call sequence are the same.
A guarantee of exact theoretical frequencies.
A generator that ignores its parameters.
questions.explanation: A seed initializes a deterministic pseudo-random process.

questions.prompt: Why should distribution parameters be chosen carefully?
questions.answer: They encode the assumptions and scale of the model.
options: They encode the assumptions and scale of the model.
They only change the printed format.
They guarantee a fixed sample mean.
They remove the need to validate data.
questions.explanation: Parameters define the distribution being modeled.

questions.prompt: Which check is generally robust for a generated sample?
questions.answer: Check its shape and valid range.
options: Require the sample mean to equal the theoretical mean exactly.
Check its shape and valid range.
Assume every generated value is unique.
Expect the same values from different seeds.
questions.explanation: Shape and support constraints are stable properties.

questions.prompt: What does sampling without replacement mean?
questions.answer: The same population item cannot be selected more than once in that sample.
options: The same population item cannot be selected more than once in that sample.
Every possible item must be selected.
The sample must be sorted.
The generator cannot use a seed.
questions.explanation: Without replacement, selected population members are not repeated.

questions.prompt: What is an important limitation of a finite random sample?
questions.answer: Observed frequencies and statistics can differ from theoretical values.
options: It always contains invalid values.
Observed frequencies and statistics can differ from theoretical values.
It cannot be reproduced with a seed.
It must have a normal distribution.
questions.explanation: Finite samples naturally vary around theoretical expectations.
